food_cultures.notes_en: One of the municipality's strongest producer-and-visit themes.

food_cultures.summary_en: Kinoshitaen makes Tokyo Black Tea from tea grown and processed in Higashiyamato. The brand revives Japanese black-tea production using local expertise in green tea.

facts.claim_en: Kinoshitaen produces the 東京紅茶 brand alongside green tea at its Higashiyamato operation.
The producer dates its revival of domestic black tea to 2001.

places.relation_en: Producer and local sales site for Tokyo Black Tea.

makers.relation_en: Grower, processor and brand owner of Tokyo Black Tea.

food_cultures.notes_en: A named Tokyo tea brand with a directly identified local producer.

food_cultures.name_ja: 杉本園 東大和紅茶
food_cultures.summary_en: Sugimotoen offers a black tea named explicitly for Higashiyamato. It represents another local interpretation of Japanese black-tea production distinct from Kinoshitaen's Tokyo Black Tea.

facts.claim_en: Sugimotoen lists 東大和紅茶 in both loose-leaf and tea-bag forms among its own products.

places.relation_en: Local maker and shop selling Higashiyamato Black Tea.

makers.relation_en: Producer of Higashiyamato Black Tea.

food_cultures.notes_en: A separate local black-tea brand from Kinoshitaen's 東京紅茶.

food_cultures.name_ja: 幸右衛門茶舗の茶づくり
food_cultures.summary_en: Founded in 1780, Kouemon maintains a long-standing tea-making tradition in Higashiyamato. Its estate links tea fields, a historic merchant identity and a contemporary cafe.

facts.claim_en: Kouemon dates its founding to 1780 and identifies its business with the Tokyo Sayama tea tradition.
Its main shop stands among tea fields and has an adjacent cafe called Café de 幸右衛門.

places.name_ja: 幸右衛門茶舗 本店
places.relation_en: Historic tea merchant's principal shop in the tea-growing landscape.
Cafe beside the tea merchant's main shop.

makers.relation_en: Historic Tokyo Sayama tea producer.

food_cultures.notes_en: Particularly suitable for a producer-centered cultural visit.

food_cultures.name_ja: 幸右衛門茶舗のフレーバー紅茶
food_cultures.summary_en: Kouemon also makes its own flavored black teas. These products demonstrate how a historic Sayama tea merchant has diversified its tea culture.

facts.claim_en: Kouemon identifies its flavored black teas as original products made by the historic tea shop.

places.name_ja: 幸右衛門茶舗 本店
places.relation_en: Producer's shop featuring its tea range.

makers.relation_en: Creator of original flavored black teas.

food_cultures.notes_en: A distinct contemporary tea product range from the producer's traditional green tea.

food_cultures.name_ja: 木下園の烏龍茶・釜炒茶
food_cultures.summary_en: Kinoshitaen produces more than green and black tea, including oolong and pan-fired teas. These varieties show the diversity of processing techniques practiced by a local tea grower.

facts.claim_en: A profile of Kinoshitaen identifies oolong and pan-fired tea among the teas produced by the historic Higashiyamato farm.

places.relation_en: Producer of several locally processed tea styles.

makers.relation_en: Tea grower and processor.

food_cultures.notes_en: Grouped as a tea-processing tradition rather than assuming each variety has a separate local origin.

food_cultures.name_ja: ひがしやまと茶うどん
food_cultures.summary_en: Tea udon combines locally produced Sayama tea powder with Higashiyamato's long-standing udon culture. It was developed by the local chamber of commerce as a modern specialty.

facts.claim_en: The Higashiyamato Chamber of Commerce developed tea udon using local Sayama tea and the area's traditional udon food culture.
facts.source_title: ひがしやまと茶うどん

facts.claim_en: Sugimotoen lists Higashiyamato Tea Udon among its products.

places.relation_en: Identified local retailer of tea udon.

makers.relation_en: Organization that developed the local tea-udon specialty.

food_cultures.notes_en: A documented fusion of a local crop and a historic dish.

food_cultures.name_ja: 東大和の郷土食・うどん
food_cultures.summary_en: Udon was historically central to family meals in Higashiyamato, especially on ceremonial occasions. It provides the culinary background for the city's modern tea-udon specialty.

facts.claim_en: The chamber of commerce records a custom of serving udon at the end of meals for weddings, funerals and other major family occasions.
facts.source_title: ひがしやまと茶うどん

facts.claim_en: A local historical archive describes handmade and simmered udon as festive foods prepared in older village households.

food_cultures.season_en: Traditionally associated with family ceremonies and special occasions.
food_cultures.notes_en: This is a documented historical household food custom, not a claim that a particular restaurant preserves the original recipe.

food_cultures.summary_en: Tokyo Cola is a green carbonated drink made using Tokyo-grown green tea. Developed by Higashiyamato producer Kinoshitaen, it combines local tea cultivation with a modern soft drink.

facts.claim_en: Tokyo's official souvenir project identifies Tokyo Cola as a Higashiyamato product made by Kinoshitaen using Tokyo-grown green tea.
TOKYO GROWN describes the beverage as a tea-based carbonated drink produced by the local tea maker.

places.relation_en: Developer and producer-associated shop for Tokyo Cola.

makers.relation_en: Local tea producer behind Tokyo Cola.

food_cultures.notes_en: A strong contemporary product with Tokyo Metropolitan Government recognition.

food_cultures.name_ja: 杉本園の狭山茶ジェラート
food_cultures.summary_en: Sugimotoen transforms its tea-making identity into gelato in roasted green tea, sencha and black tea varieties. The sweets connect a traditional local producer to contemporary food tourism.

facts.claim_en: Sugimotoen lists original gelato varieties made with hojicha, sencha and black tea.

places.relation_en: Tea producer and identified seller of the three gelato varieties.

makers.relation_en: Producer-associated brand of tea gelato.

food_cultures.notes_en: The producer confirms the product range; it does not specify the source of every non-tea ingredient.

food_cultures.name_ja: けやきリーフの堅焼きパイ
food_cultures.summary_en: A crisp pastry shaped after the zelkova leaf, a symbol of Higashiyamato. It incorporates locally produced Sayama tea powder.

facts.claim_en: The Higashiyamato Chamber of Commerce identifies this zelkova-leaf pastry as a confection made with Higashiyamato-grown Sayama tea powder.
facts.source_title: 狭山茶パウダーのお菓子

places.relation_en: Sales agent identified for the tea-powder confection.

makers.name_ja: お菓子工房Laboふたりしまい
makers.relation_en: Confectioner making the pastry with local tea powder.

food_cultures.notes_en: The documented maker is based in neighboring Musashimurayama; the connection to Higashiyamato is the local tea ingredient and city-symbol design. Current availability is not independently verified.

food_cultures.summary_en: A lightly bitter-sweet meringue confection made with Higashiyamato Sayama tea powder. It is part of a product-development initiative extending local tea beyond beverages.

facts.claim_en: Chameringue is a meringue sweet using Sayama tea powder produced in Higashiyamato.
facts.source_title: 狭山茶パウダーのお菓子

places.relation_en: Sales agent listed for the local-tea meringues.

makers.name_ja: お菓子工房Laboふたりしまい
makers.relation_en: Maker of the tea-powder meringue.

food_cultures.notes_en: The confectioner is based outside Higashiyamato, but the tea ingredient is explicitly local. Current availability is unverified.

food_cultures.summary_en: Tamako Pears are a regional fruit identity shared by Higashiyamato and neighboring Higashimurayama. Their name refers to nearby Lake Tama, and the designation covers several pear varieties.

facts.claim_en: Higashiyamato City identifies pears grown around Higashiyamato and Higashimurayama as 多摩湖梨 because of their proximity to Lake Tama.
The regional pear designation includes varieties such as Kosui, Hosui and Inagi.

places.relation_en: The municipality documents a network of direct-sales sites where locally grown fruit may be encountered seasonally.

makers.name_ja: 東大和市内の梨生産農家
makers.relation_en: Local growers of Tamako Pears.

food_cultures.notes_en: A named regional fruit identity, not a single pear variety. No individual producing orchard was verified.

food_cultures.summary_en: Daikon is Higashiyamato's leading vegetable by both cultivated area and harvest volume. It has a longstanding role in the city's urban agriculture.

facts.claim_en: The municipality identifies daikon as its largest vegetable crop by both planted area and harvested amount.

places.name_ja: 東大和市内農産物直売所
places.relation_en: Direct-sales network for locally harvested vegetables.

food_cultures.notes_en: No claim is made that this is a distinct historical daikon cultivar.

food_cultures.summary_en: Potatoes are cultivated by many Higashiyamato farmers. The municipality specifically identifies Danshaku and Kitaakari among its common varieties.

facts.claim_en: Higashiyamato City identifies potatoes as a crop grown by many local farmers, particularly the Danshaku and Kitaakari varieties.

places.name_ja: 東大和市内農産物直売所
places.relation_en: Municipally documented network of local farm outlets.
places.address_ja: 東京都東大和市内各所

food_cultures.notes_en: A documented local crop rather than an exclusive Higashiyamato variety.

food_cultures.summary_en: Spinach is a representative leafy vegetable of Higashiyamato's urban farms. The city describes its cultivation as spanning the year.

facts.claim_en: The municipality identifies spinach as a representative locally grown vegetable cultivated throughout the year.

places.name_ja: 東大和市内農産物直売所
places.relation_en: Local farm-product sales network.
places.address_ja: 東京都東大和市内各所

food_cultures.notes_en: The source supports local production but not a unique named cultivar.

food_cultures.summary_en: Sweet potatoes remain part of Higashiyamato's agricultural identity and crop-harvest experiences. Historic accounts also describe their importance as everyday food in older local villages.

facts.claim_en: The municipality identifies sweet potatoes as a locally grown crop associated with harvest activities.
Historical accounts describe boiled sweet potatoes as an important everyday food in the villages associated with the present Lake Tama area.

places.name_ja: 東大和市内農産物直売所
places.relation_en: Local outlets for crops grown in the municipality.
places.address_ja: 東京都東大和市内各所

food_cultures.notes_en: The historical account supplies additional cultural depth beyond the present crop listing.

food_cultures.summary_en: Alongside Tamako Pears, Higashiyamato farms produce grapes, mandarins, blueberries and apples. These fruits form part of the city's smaller-scale direct-sale agricultural landscape.

facts.claim_en: Higashiyamato City identifies grapes, mandarins, blueberries and apples among fruits harvested in the municipality.
The municipality documents a network of local direct-sales outlets that includes seasonal fruit.

places.name_ja: 東大和市内農産物直売所
places.relation_en: Network of outlets for seasonal fruit and other locally harvested produce.
places.address_ja: 東京都東大和市内各所

food_cultures.notes_en: Grouped because the municipal source documents these crops collectively without establishing separate named regional varieties.

food_cultures.summary_en: Before the creation of Lake Tama, households in the affected villages relied heavily on barley-based meals. Cracked barley, sometimes mixed with smaller quantities of rice or millet, was an everyday staple.

facts.claim_en: A historical account of villages submerged by the Murayama Reservoir describes cracked-barley rice and barley-based meals as everyday staples.

food_cultures.notes_en: Historical food culture documented through a local archive; no contemporary establishment offering a reconstruction was verified.

food_cultures.summary_en: Bakumeshi was a slowly cooked dish of whole barley, sometimes eaten with miso soup or daikon. It reflects a period when barley was more accessible than polished rice.

facts.claim_en: The local historical archive describes bakumeshi as whole barley cooked until soft and sometimes served with miso soup or daikon.

food_cultures.notes_en: A historical household dish, not a verified current menu item.

food_cultures.summary_en: Households in the older Higashiyamato area supplemented staple meals with dumplings cooked in broth. Recorded versions include wheat-flour dumplings and a soup using barley-flour dumplings.

facts.claim_en: The local historical archive documents 煮だんご, comparable to suiton, and だんご汁 made with barley-flour dumplings.

food_cultures.notes_en: Historical food preparations associated with the older village economy. No present-day tasting venue was established.

food_cultures.name_ja: やきもち・たらしもち
food_cultures.summary_en: Yaki-mochi, also called tarashi-mochi locally, was made from flattened wheat-flour dough cooked on a metal pan and flavored with soy sauce and sugar.

facts.claim_en: The historical archive records a local wheat-flour cake called やきもち or たらしもち, cooked on both sides and seasoned with soy sauce and sugar.

food_cultures.notes_en: A documented historic preparation without a verified contemporary commercial example.

food_cultures.summary_en: Ude-manjyu was a boiled wheat-based bun recorded among the older village foods of the Higashiyamato area. It formed part of a wider flour-based food culture.

facts.claim_en: The local historical archive identifies うでまんじゅう as a boiled bun prepared in older village households.

food_cultures.notes_en: Historical documentation only; ingredients beyond the broader flour-food context and modern availability were not established.
